description: The app frame inset: the CSS custom properties a host client publishes on the Control UI's root at document start, and the injected rule that puts the page inside them. Two groups, one script: the page's viewport-ANCHORED overlays are inset into the frame with block-axis margins, which cannot over-constrain a box the page anchored by one of its own edges, and the page's own viewport-HEIGHT containers are bounded by the frame's height, which is the only half an in-flow box needs. This file is the ONE owner of the property names, the marker attribute, the setter global, both selector groups and the injected script: core/app-frame-inset.js reads it (the desktop installs the script into the gateway page from its preload at document start; the iOS client bundles THIS FILE and installs it through a WKUserScript at document start), so there is one copy in the tree rather than one per client. The rule itself is built by the script from the fields here, so no client reimplements it.
why: The two halves of this. A host client already OWNS its chrome geometrically: the desktop's title strip and notice banner are separate child views with their own rectangles, and the gateway page view is inset below the strip by layoutViews(), so nothing the page paints can land on them. That half is done and is not to be fought with z-index, overlays or modals. What is missing is the other half: the PAGE does not know that region exists. It measures window.innerHeight and anchors its overlays to the display edges, so a full-bleed surface is drawn across the band the client's own chrome occupies. This publishes the missing fact.

Why custom properties rather than a stylesheet the client keeps in sync. The inset has to reach the page's OWN layout decisions, and the page is upstream and free to change its markup at any release. A published value it can read is the same contract the W3C safe-area tokens already are, and it survives a rename of any element the page draws. The client that knows the region publishes it, and the page's overlays land inside it.

★ Why a published value is not enough on its own, and the clamp exists. Publishing a variable changes nothing by itself: the page's overlays are position: fixed with geometry computed in JS from window.innerHeight and window.innerWidth (the assistant panel is the case that was reported, 80% of the inner height by default and full-viewport on a narrow display), so the values it uses never pass through a custom property. The rule the script builds is what makes the published value bind: it moves the block-axis edges of the page's viewport-anchored overlays onto the frame and caps their height at the frame's own height.

★ The 100vh stragglers, and why the cap is in dvh. On a phone 100vh is the LARGEST viewport, taller than the visible screen, so a box sized that way is already taller than the display before any frame is taken off it. dvh tracks the visible region, so the cap is written in dvh with the frame insets subtracted. A box whose own height is under that cap is untouched, which is what leaves a docked and resized panel its own size rather than forcing every surface to fill the frame.

★ Why the rule is gated on a MARKER rather than applied unconditionally. On the desktop the page's viewport is already the region below the strip, so the frame insets are zero and there is nothing to clamp. An unconditional rule would still rewrite the panel's own block-axis edges, and a bottom-docked panel carries both edges, so the over-constrained case resolves to the top edge and pulls it to the top of the window. That is a regression on the client that does not need the clamp, so the script sets the marker on the root only while a client publishes a frame that takes space, and everything else is left exactly as the page set it.

★ Why the page's OWN viewport-height container is named here and not only its overlays. A client that insets the page's content pads the body by the safe area, and the page's own root container is sized in dvh, which is the DISPLAY rather than the padded box: the shell therefore starts at the top inset and ends past the bottom edge of the screen, by exactly the top inset. Its block-end content, the composer cluster among it, is then drawn in the home-indicator band and cut off by the screen edge, which is what a reader reports as a composer going off the bottom. The height cap in this rule is what bounds it, and it does the work on an in-flow box on its own: top and bottom are inert on a positioned-static box, while max-height applies to it, so one declaration bounds a docked overlay and the page shell alike. Measured at a 390x844 viewport with the frame published as top 59 and bottom 34: the shell ran 59 to 903 and the composer's action row at 810 to 846, so 36px of the row sat in the home-indicator band and its last 2px past the display; with the cap it ends at 810.

Why the clamp is the BLOCK axis only. Those are the edges a phone's chrome and the desktop's banner band take. The inline axis is left as the page set it, because a docked panel carries its own inline placement and a rule that rewrote it would move a panel the reader docked on purpose.

Why document start. The panel's geometry is computed as it renders, and a rule added after the first paint is a visible jump from full bleed to bounded. The same timing and the same reason as the client-context hook and the pairing observer: installed late it races a layout the page has already done, and the frames it missed are silent.

Why a setter and not only an install-time value. The client's own chrome changes while the page is open: a notice banner appears and takes a band at the top, and goes away again. The published values have to move with it, so the script leaves a plain writable global the client calls, and the client pushes the new numbers from the layout pass it already runs. Re-installing is not needed and the setter is idempotent.

The panel is the reported case, not the only one. The rule names the page's viewport-anchored overlays: the assistant panel host and its body, and the two full-viewport unavailable surfaces. They are named because CSS cannot select on a computed position, and the list is deliberately short: anything not anchored to the display edges keeps its own geometry.

THE REMOVAL TRIGGER: delete this once the Control UI takes its own insets from the host, meaning it reads a published frame region for its overlays rather than window.innerHeight. At that point the page is bounded by its own contract and this is one more rule over someone else's markup. What retires it is an upstream Control UI release carrying that behaviour, not a date. Removal is the files plus every pointer: core/spec/app-frame-inset.json, core/app-frame-inset.js and its tests, the mobile project resource entry, the WKUserScript registration, the desktop preload channel and its guard test.
script: // The rule is built HERE rather than by each client, so the one copy of the
// clamp is this file and a client only ever hands over its own numbers.
for (var i = 0; i < SELECTORS.length; i++) selectors.push(marker + ' ' + SELECTORS[i]);
for (var j = 0; j < BOUND_SELECTORS.length; j++) bounded.push(marker + ' ' + BOUND_SELECTORS[j]);
var cap = 'max-height: calc(100dvh - var(' + PROPS.top + ', 0px) - var(' + PROPS.bottom + ', 0px)) !important;';
// An in-flow container is bounded by the edges the frame takes off the side it
// starts from, because that is the whole of what it overflows by: its block-end
// content clears the far edge through the page's own safe-area tokens, so
// subtracting that edge here would take the same band off twice.
var n = typeof value === 'number' ? value : parseFloat(value);
// Returns whether the published frame takes any space at all, which is the
// same question as whether the clamp applies. Idempotent, so a client that
// pushes the same numbers on every layout pass costs one attribute read.
window.__clawFrameInset = { set: set, properties: PROPS, marker: MARKER };
